subject: history_social
passage: The Inca recorded information on khipus, bundles of knotted cords in which the position and type of each knot stood for a number. Specialists known as khipukamayuq kept the cords and could read from them the contents of storehouses or the labor owed by a village. After the Spanish conquest in the 1530s, these records did not vanish at once. For several decades, Spanish officials in some regions accepted the testimony of khipu keepers, who read from their cords what tribute a community had paid, and clerks wrote it down. Only later, as the colonial administration grew suspicious of records it could not itself read, did the khipu fall out of official use.
stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

choices.A: It argues that Spanish officials never understood Inca record keeping.
choices.B: It describes an Inca practice and then explains why the Spanish immediately banned it.
choices.C: It explains how to read a khipu and then compares it with written records.
choices.D: It describes a record-keeping system and then traces how its official use continued for a time before ending.

explanation.why: The first two sentences describe the khipu system. The third says the records "did not vanish at once," and the fourth describes decades of continued use under Spanish rule. The last sentence explains how official use finally ended. The text describes a system and follows its fate over time.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says officials accepted khipu testimony for decades; it argues nothing about their level of understanding.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the records "did not vanish at once" and were used for decades, so there was no immediate ban.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text gives only a brief idea of how knots stood for numbers and does not compare khipus with written records.
explanation.D: Correct. The text explains what khipus were and then traces their continued acceptance under Spanish officials until suspicion ended their official use.
